Strategy B on the football graph (context on)¶

Strategy B is a single-turn agent: the model plans up to 3 web searches (Ollama web search), reads the top results (evidence capped at 3,000 tokens) and answers with citations. Two variants on the same retrieval: search (search_evidence: answer from the evidence only) and search + memory (search_memory: the synthesis call replayed on the same evidence, now allowing the model's own knowledge). 5 models, 3 runs each, 239 context-on tasks (football-v1-ctx-idmix).

Scoring. Each task hides one property. The answer of a configuration (model, prompt or approach) is the vote over its 3 runs (text: most frequent value; numbers: mean; abstained only when all 3 runs abstain), and is correct, wrong or abstained. F1 = 2c / (2c + 2w + a) counts abstentions against recall; F1 (abstentions ignored) = 2c / (2c + w) scores only the answers given (the paper's Table 3 scoring). Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over tasks (1,000 resamples); paired differences resample the same tasks for both sides; task-by-task comparisons use an exact McNemar test on "correct".

On football, Strategy B answers few tasks and is right on about a quarter of the answers. With search only, F1 is 0.07–0.17 and abstention 54–87%; precision is 0.22–0.29 for every model. Allowing the model's memory on the same evidence raises F1 to 0.12–0.23 and F1 ign to 0.43–0.51, mostly by lowering abstention by 2–14 points. deepseek-v4.1-flash is the most cautious agent (87% abstention with search, 79% with memory).

Memory improves both scores for every model. F1 rises by 0.04–0.07 and F1 ign by 0.05–0.08, but the intervals overlap because each model answers only 31–141 of the 239 tasks. The ranking by F1 follows the ranking by abstention: mistral (lowest abstention, 41% with memory) has the best F1, deepseek (79%) the worst. On F1 ign the five models are within 0.08 of each other.

Wrong answers outnumber right ones 2–4 to 1 for every model and both variants. Memory moves tasks out of the abstained share into both the correct and the wrong share, so its benefit for F1 comes with more wrong answers. The agent does not become more accurate when allowed to use memory; it becomes less cautious.

Precision against recall: what memory changes¶

In [5]:
t = metrics(B, ["model", "approach"]).set_index(["model", "approach"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.5))

In precision–recall space, memory moves every model up and to the right: recall rises by 0.03–0.06 and precision by 0.03–0.06. No model trades precision for recall, which means the extra answers from memory are at least as accurate as the evidence-only ones.

Task by task, the gain from memory comes almost entirely from tasks that search left unanswered. Between 8 and 15 of them become correct, but 13–21 become wrong. Tasks answered correctly with search rarely change (0–8 lost). The gain in correct answers is significant for gemma4 (p = 0.002), mistral (p = 0.001) and deepseek (p = 0.008), but not for gpt-oss:20b (p = 0.08) and gpt-oss:120b (p = 0.12).

Even when memory is allowed, 86–98% of the answers still cite the evidence. The 2–14% that cite nothing (answers from memory) are more precise (0.37–0.67) than the cited ones (0.26–0.31). The model's knowledge is more reliable than the retrieved pages for the few facts it is confident about; the retrieved pages are often about another player.

3. Retrieval¶

The search plan names the right player only when the name is in the given properties: in 92.6% of those runs against 0.2% of the runs without a name. Without a name, the planner searches for generic statistics ("goalkeeper clean sheets") and 84% of those runs abstain. With the right player identified, the answers become frequent but are still mostly wrong (45% wrong vs 11% correct when the name is given). Even with the right page, extracting the exact season statistic stored in the graph is hard.

The evidence comes from a long tail of 1,174 distinct domains; the top 5 hold only 30% of the evidence slots. fbref.com, which is the likely origin of the football dataset, is the most frequent source (3,404 runs) but is cited by only 220 answers. Many results are aggregator or statistics sites whose numbers belong to a different season or competition than the graph.

The 3,000-token evidence cap is reached in 54–100% of runs, so the synthesis model usually sees truncated evidence. With 0–2 evidence items no model answers. With 3 or more, answer rates are 15–33% (gemma4 reaches 67% at 7+ items). More evidence makes answering more likely but not more accurate.

Strategy B's scores barely depend on the strata on football. Pooled over models, search-only F1 is 0.11–0.17 in every stratum of H, G and node centrality, and memory adds 0.02–0.08 everywhere. The popularity effect seen for B on airports (high-pop H much easier) does not appear: football statistics are equally hard to retrieve whatever their popularity.

The name changes how often B answers, not how often it is right. In the 81 high-G tasks, abstention falls from 75% (search) and 67% (memory) without name or team to 28% and 10% with both. F1 roughly doubles (0.10 → 0.21 with search, 0.08 → 0.26 with memory), but F1 ign does not rise (0.40 → 0.41 and 0.29 → 0.43, intervals overlapping). The name gets the agent to the right page, where it then often reads the wrong value.

Minutes per start (F1 ign 0.93 with memory) is again the easiest property, since a typical value passes the tolerance. Position is almost never right with B (1 of 71 answers), because the evidence and the models use words ("Goalkeeper", "central midfielder") where the ground truth uses codes ("GK", "DF,MF"). This is a format limit of the token-overlap scoring rather than a retrieval failure.

As for Strategy A, the wrong numeric answers of B are far from the truth (median relative error about 1), but fewer of them are a default 0 (6% with search, 14% with memory, against 38% for A). B's wrong numbers are mostly real values read from the wrong page, season or competition.

5. Stability and effort¶

Agreement of the 3 runs¶

The 3 runs agree on the outcome for 56–62% of the tasks for the gpt-oss models and 61–68% for mistral. deepseek (84–90%) and gemma4 (74–80%) agree more often, mainly because they abstain consistently. Memory slightly lowers agreement for four of five models: the answers from memory vary more between runs than the decision to abstain.

A search run costs 0.36 Wh (gemma4) to 1.58 Wh (mistral), of which the web searches (1.2–3.0 per run, 0.3 Wh each) are 58–98%. Input is about 3,400–3,700 tokens, almost all of it evidence, which gives a token amplification of 6.3–7.0×. The memory variant reuses the same retrieval, so its marginal cost is one more synthesis call; the totals shown count the searches again, as a stand-alone run would.

Takeaways¶

  1. Strategy B is weak on football: F1 0.07–0.17 with search only and 0.12–0.23 with memory, with precision about 0.25–0.34; most tasks are abstained (41–87%).
  2. Memory helps every model (+0.04–0.07 F1, +0.05–0.08 F1 ign; significant for 3 of 5 models). It does so by answering tasks that search left open, which become correct or wrong in roughly equal numbers.
  3. Identification is the bottleneck. Without the player's name, the plan names the right player in 0.2% of runs. With the name, it does in 93%, but precision does not improve, because the retrieved statistics belong to other seasons or competitions.
  4. Sources are scattered and noisy: 1,174 domains; even the likely source of the dataset (fbref.com) gives precision 0.35.
  5. Answers from memory are rare but more precise (0.37–0.67) than cited ones (0.26–0.31).
  6. B costs 0.36–1.58 Wh per run, 58–98% of it in searches, with a token amplification of 6.3–7.0×.
